related_questions.question: What is the difference between an attorney and an attorney at law?

text_blocks.snippet: The terms "attorney" and "attorney at law" are essentially interchangeable and refer to the same thing: a licensed legal professional who has completed law school and passed a bar exam to practice law. While "attorney" is a shortened version of "attorney at law," they both denote someone qualified to represent clients in legal proceedings and provide legal advice.

list.title: Lawyer vs. Attorney:
list.snippet: The term "lawyer" is broader and can refer to someone with a law degree who may or may not be licensed to practice in court. An "attorney" or "attorney at law," however, is a lawyer who has passed the bar exam and is licensed to represent clients in court and provide legal services.

list.title: "Attorney at Law" as the Full Term:
list.snippet: The term "attorney at law" is the more formal and complete title, while "attorney" is a more casual shorthand.

list.title: Licensing and Practice:
list.snippet: The key distinction lies in the licensing. To be an attorney at law, one must pass a state bar exam and be admitted to the bar, allowing them to practice law, including appearing in court.
